title: Pyridoxal photoenzymes for asymmetric radical-radical cross-couplings.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Opened the Europe PMC/PMC record for PMC13538046 and read the data availability statement verbatim: 'The data that support the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author upon request.' Listed the article's attached files from the PMC article page: exactly two, both PDF (Supplementary Information, 38.3 MB, 'sections 1-7, Supplementary Figs. 1-46 and Supplementary Table 1'; Peer Review File, 5.5 MB). No .csv, .tsv, .xlsx or .zip is attached. Queried the PMC open-access package service (HTTP 404, no bulk package). Searched Zenodo for the DOI: 0 records. Checked the one text-mined accession, Protein Data Bank entry 9E97, via the RCSB and PDBe REST APIs: it is a crystal structure of a Thermotoga maritima L-allo-threonine aldolase mutant deposited 2024-11-07 whose primary citation is a different 2025 J. Am. Chem. Soc. paper, so it is cited background, not this paper's data.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: Everything about the chemistry itself (that pyridoxal 5'-phosphate, a vitamin-B6-derived enzyme cofactor, acts as a light-driven single-electron donor; the substrate scope; the yields and enantiomeric excess values; the enzyme variants used) comes from the abstract and the article's front matter. Europe PMC carries only the abstract, acknowledgements, data availability and references for this article (CC BY-NC-ND licence), so I never saw the results body, and I never opened the 38.3 MB Supplementary Information PDF because no machine-readable table exists inside it to open.

a1_downloadable.note: FAIL, and this is the killer. The data availability statement says the data are 'available from the corresponding author upon request', which the checklist lists as an automatic A1 failure. Confirmed by file inspection, not inference: the only two downloadable artifacts are a 38.3 MB Supplementary Information PDF and a 5.5 MB Peer Review File PDF. No dataset in Zenodo, no PMC open-access package (404), and the single Protein Data Bank entry found in the text (9E97) belongs to an earlier paper by the same lab.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: FAIL. The only plausible labels (percentage yield and enantiomeric excess, a measure of how much one mirror-image product dominates) exist as numbers printed under chemical structure drawings in figures and in one Supplementary Table inside a PDF. They are not a column in any file; building a label table would mean transcribing a PDF by hand.

a3_inputs_present.note: FAIL. The inputs would be substrate chemical structures and enzyme variant sequences. Substrates appear only as drawn structures in figures, with no SMILES (a text encoding of a molecule) anywhere machine-readable; enzyme variants are named by mutation codes in the text, not supplied as sequences.

a4_units_stated.note: Not reached in practice, but the field's conventions are unambiguous: yield and enantiomeric excess are both reported in percent. Taken from the paper's conventions, not from an opened file.

a5_enough_rows.note: FAIL on the available evidence. The entire supplement contains one Supplementary Table and 46 figures; a Nature synthetic-chemistry substrate scope is typically a few dozen entries, far under the ~400-row floor for classification. I did not count the entries, so n_rows is null rather than a guessed number.

a6_fits_laptop.note: Trivially laptop-sized. This is the only Part A item that passes comfortably, and it passes because there is almost no data.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Cannot be assessed: there is no download whose counts could be compared against the paper. Recorded as a fail because the check is impossible, not because a disagreement was found.

a8_label_provenance.note: Label provenance is actually clean in principle: yields and enantiomeric excess are direct physical measurements (chromatography on isolated products), not another model's output and not computable from the features. This is the one genuine strength of the underlying measurements, and it is wasted because they are not released.

existing_models.name: Random-forest model for amidase enantioselectivity (Nature Communications 2024, 'Machine learning-assisted amidase-catalytic enantioselectivity prediction and rational design of variants')
existing_models.score_and_split: Retrieved as a search result only; the summary states 240 reaction datasets were used to train random-forest classifiers of enantioselectivity and that the best designed variant gave a 53-fold higher E-value than wild type. I did not open the paper, so I cannot state its metric or split.

backbone.name: ChemBERTa or MolFormer (molecule language models) for substrates, plus ESM-2 (a protein language model) for enzyme variants
backbone.hardware: Would run on a laptop CPU for a few dozen molecules, but there is no label table to fit a head to.
backbone.licence: Backbone licences are permissive; irrelevant here. The article itself is CC BY-NC-ND, which also restricts redistributing adapted material.

integration.partner_dataset: None usable. In principle a substrate-scope table carrying SMILES could join to PubChem or ChEMBL on InChIKey, and the enzyme variants to UniProt via the Thermotoga maritima threonine aldolase parent sequence.
integration.join_key: InChIKey (molecules) / UniProt accession (enzyme) — neither identifier is present in any released file.
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Cannot be written against this paper's data, because no released file contains either key.

controls.positive_control: Would have been: predict molecular weight from the substrate structure, which must come out near-perfect. Not runnable, as no structures are released in machine-readable form.
controls.negative_control: Label shuffling; not runnable without labels.
controls.external_validation: The Hyster lab's own earlier photobiocatalysis papers (for example the 2024 Nature paper on stereoselective amino acid synthesis by photobiocatalytic oxidative coupling) would be the natural second source, but they share the same problem: numbers live in PDFs.

honest_claim_h3: No claim is possible from this paper's released files; the only downloadable artifacts are two PDFs, and the measurements behind every yield and enantioselectivity number are explicitly held by the corresponding author on request.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use substrate structure and enzyme variant identity to predict the yield and mirror-image purity of a light-driven enzymatic coupling reaction.
plain_idea.train_on: Each example would be one reaction: the chemical structure of the amine starting material, the structure of the radical partner, and which engineered enzyme variant was used. The number of examples is unknown and almost certainly a few dozen, because the entire supplement holds one table and 46 figures.
plain_idea.predict: Percentage yield and enantiomeric excess (how strongly one mirror-image form of the product dominates). The true answers come from the authors' own chromatography on isolated products, which is a direct physical measurement.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: If it worked at scale, biocatalysis groups such as the Hyster lab at Princeton and process chemists at Novartis could rank candidate substrates before running them, saving lab weeks. At the size actually available it would only tell us that a few dozen reactions cannot train a model.

more_or_better_data.why: The one model I retrieved (a 2024 random-forest enantioselectivity predictor for amidases) was reportedly trained on 240 reactions. This paper releases zero machine-readable reactions, so our data would be smaller by construction, not larger.

confidence_score.why: No replicate measurements or per-reaction error bars are released, so there is nothing from which to estimate noise and give calibrated per-prediction confidence.

models_beatable.why: Irrelevant here: with no training table we could not fit anything to compare. I also did not open the 2024 amidase paper, so I cannot honestly judge its split or strength.

guaranteed_improvement.why: Fails the first condition outright: there is no dataset to join to, no join key in any released file, and no baseline we could run on a shared split.

ml_idea: The idea considered was a reaction-outcome model: embed the amine substrate and radical precursor with a molecule language model such as ChemBERTa, embed the engineered threonine aldolase variant with the protein language model ESM-2, and fit a small head to predict yield and enantiomeric excess, held out by substrate scaffold. It dies before it starts, because the paper releases its measurements only on request and prints them inside a 38.3 MB PDF.

effort.compute_note: No compute estimate is meaningful: there is no feature/label table and no path to one short of manually transcribing a PDF and redrawing every substrate as SMILES. The 44 MB figure is the total size of the two attached PDFs, read from the PMC article page.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Read the data availability statement and list the attached files — two minutes. It says 'available from the corresponding author upon request' and the attachments are two PDFs. Do this before anything else on any synthetic-chemistry paper.

verdict_reason: Part A1 fails outright: the data are 'available from the corresponding author upon request', and the only downloadable files are a 38.3 MB Supplementary Information PDF (46 figures, one table) and a 5.5 MB peer review PDF, with nothing in Zenodo, no PMC open-access package, and the single Protein Data Bank entry in the text belonging to an earlier paper. A2 and A3 fail with it, since both the labels (yield, enantiomeric excess) and the inputs (substrate structures) exist only as drawings and numbers inside a PDF, and A5 almost certainly fails too at a few dozen reactions. The underlying measurements are exactly the kind an ML project wants — direct physical readouts, no model-derived labels — which makes this a genuinely frustrating reject rather than a bad paper.
